facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; South Carolina ratified the U.S. Constitution on May 23, 1788, the 8th state to do so.
facts.motto: Two mottos: Dum spiro spero ("While I breathe, I hope") and Animis opibusque parati ("Prepared in mind and resources")

symbols.name: Palmetto (1939); in 1776 a fort built of palmetto logs on Sullivan's Island held off a British naval attack

facts.name_origin: Carolina comes from Carolus, the Latin form of Charles, for King Charles I of England.

government.legislature: South Carolina General Assembly (the state legislature), which meets in the State House in Columbia
government.chambers: South Carolina Senate (46 senators, 4-year terms) and South Carolina House of Representatives (124 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no one may be elected governor for more than two terms in a row). The governor is elected directly by the voters (direct election of the governor began with the 1865 constitution) and leads the executive branch.
government.courts: South Carolina Supreme Court (5 justices: a Chief Justice and four Associate Justices, 10-year terms). Unusually, South Carolina's justices and judges are elected by the General Assembly in a joint vote of both chambers.
government.constitution: The current constitution was adopted in 1895, during a time when leaders worked to take away the votes of Black citizens and poor white citizens through literacy tests and property rules. Earlier constitutions came in 1776, 1778, 1790, 1865, and 1868; the 1868 constitution was written by the only state convention in the South with a majority of Black delegates, and it ended debtors' prison, overturned the Black Codes, and set up public schools.
government.kid_line: "All political power is vested in and derived from the people only." (South Carolina Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: Before Europeans came, South Carolina held many separate Native nations, including the powerful chiefdom of Cofitachequi.

The Catawba lived along the Catawba River as farmers who also fished and hunted, growing corn. Catawba women made pottery and baskets, and the Catawba have what is believed to be the oldest surviving pottery tradition east of the Mississippi.

The Cherokee Lower Towns, led by the town of Keowee, sat along the Keowee River in today's Oconee County. Cherokee families lived in wattle-and-daub houses of wood and clay with roofs of wood or thatched grass.

long_ago.nation: Cusabo peoples (including the Kiawah, Edisto, and Etiwan)
long_ago.about: The Cusabo lived in their own villages along the coast between today's Charleston and the Savannah River, and spoke a language unlike their neighbors'. Charles Town was built on Cusabo land in 1670.

long_ago.nation: Siouan-speaking nations of the coastal plain
long_ago.about: About a dozen nations of Siouan background lived up the rivers of the eastern coastal plain.
In 1715 the Yamasee led a war against the colony over the trade in enslaved Native people, cheating traders, and plantations spreading onto their land.

today.about: The only federally recognized tribe in South Carolina; ended by the U.S. government in 1959 and recognized again by Congress in 1993, with headquarters in Rock Hill and a 1,012-acre reservation in York County.

first_peoples.today_note: The Catawba Indian Nation is South Carolina's one federally recognized tribe. Many other nations were pushed out or joined larger nations after the Yamasee War; most Cusabo, for example, joined the Catawba or the Muscogee (Creek).
sites: Catawba Indian Nation lands near Rock Hill (York County)
Keowee, site of the main Cherokee Lower Town (Oconee County)
Reconstruction Era National Historical Park (Beaufort County), including Penn Center and Camp Saxton

history.event: Many Native nations live in what is now South Carolina, including the powerful chiefdom of Cofitachequi.
On October 8, Spanish colonists found San Miguel de Gualdape near today's Georgetown.
Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition passes through, recording a people called Chalaque near the Keowee River, part of the Cherokee homeland.
English settlers, many from the island of Barbados, found Charles Town on Cusabo land; the colony soon fights and defeats the Kussoe and Stono and takes much of their land.
The Yamasee War: the Yamasee, Muscogee, and others fight the colony over the trade in enslaved Native people and cheating traders. The colony wins and takes control of the coast.

Enslaved Africans are now the majority of South Carolina's people. Their skill at growing rice, brought from West Africa, makes planters rich, and the Gullah culture and language grow in the Lowcountry and Sea Islands. Almost half of all enslaved people brought into what became the U.S. arrive through Charleston.

In the Stono Rebellion (September 9), as many as 100 enslaved people near the Stono River march south toward Spanish Florida, where they hope to claim freedom. About 40 white people and probably as many Black people are killed, and the colony answers with the harsh Negro Act of 1740.
Smallpox kills nearly half of the Catawba; in 1763 the colony confirms a 225-square-mile reservation along the Catawba River.
On June 28, a fort made of palmetto logs on Sullivan's Island holds off a British naval attack; about a third of the Revolutionary War's fighting later takes place in South Carolina.
On May 23, South Carolina becomes the 8th state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Denmark Vesey, a free Black preacher in Charleston, plans an uprising. The plan is revealed, and the city hangs 35 people.
In the Treaty of Nation Ford, the state takes nearly all of the Catawba reservation, leaving one square mile.
Weeks after Abraham Lincoln's election, South Carolina becomes the first state to secede. On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor.

Union forces take Port Royal and the Sea Islands; freed people build the town of Mitchelville, and missionaries from Pennsylvania open Penn School (1862) for freed people. On May 13, 1862, Robert Smalls steers the Planter to freedom, and on January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation is read to about 3,000 people at Camp Saxton.

A convention with a Black majority writes the 1868 constitution, and South Carolina is readmitted to the Union on July 9, 1868. The state has a majority-Black government until about 1876, when voter fraud returns former Confederates to power; federal troops leave in 1877.

trailblazers.name: Eliza Lucas Pinckney
trailblazers.text: As a young woman Eliza Lucas ran her family's plantations and tested seeds her father sent from the Caribbean. In 1744 she grew enough indigo, a plant used for blue dye, to begin making dye, and by the 1770s indigo was about one third of South Carolina's exports. The work was done by enslaved people she oversaw, so her story is both one of skill and one of slavery's profits.

trailblazers.name: Sergeant William Jasper
trailblazers.text: During the 1776 British attack on the palmetto-log fort on Sullivan's Island, Jasper brought back the fort's shot-down flag. His act became a South Carolina legend.

trailblazers.name: Morris Brown
trailblazers.text: Morris Brown and other Black Methodists in Charleston founded the church that became Mother Emanuel AME, now the oldest AME church in the South.

trailblazers.name: Denmark Vesey
trailblazers.text: Vesey was a free Black preacher in Charleston who in 1822 planned an uprising. The plan was revealed before it began, and the city hanged 35 people and sent others away.

trailblazers.name: Robert Smalls
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Beaufort, Smalls and seven other enslaved crewmen took the Confederate ship Planter out of Charleston Harbor to the Union navy on May 13, 1862, carrying their families to freedom. He later served in the state legislature, wrote the law for the first free, compulsory public school system in the United States, and served in the U.S. Congress.

trailblazers.name: Septima Poinsette Clark
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, teacher and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Born in Charleston, Clark was fired by the Charleston City School Board in the 1950s after she refused to keep her NAACP membership secret. She designed programs that taught adults to read and write so they could register and vote, an idea the National Park Service calls a cornerstone of the Civil Rights Movement.

waters: Charleston Harbor and the Ashley, Cooper, and Wando rivers
geography.regions: South Carolina rises from the Atlantic Coastal Plain and Sea Islands of the Lowcountry, across the Sandhills and the Fall Line, to the Piedmont and the Blue Ridge Mountains in the Upstate.

ecosystems.name: Longleaf pine forests
ecosystems.about: Longleaf pine forests give a home to deer and songbirds.

ecosystems.name: Salt marshes, estuaries, and Sea Islands
ecosystems.about: The Lowcountry coast is lined with salt marshes, estuaries, and barrier islands, part of the historic homeland of the Gullah Geechee people.

science.weather: South Carolina has a humid subtropical climate. Major hurricanes include Hazel (1954), Hugo (1989, which hit Charleston as a Category 4 storm), Florence (2018), and Helene (2024). The 1886 Charleston earthquake was the largest ever to hit the eastern United States.
science.resources: In colonial times rice and indigo grown by enslaved Africans made planters rich, and the Fall Line was an important early source of water power. Today the economy includes aerospace (Boeing in Charleston since 2011), car making (BMW near Greer since 1994), farming (tobacco, poultry, cotton, cattle), and tourism.
science.highlight: The 1886 Charleston earthquake: on August 31, 1886, an earthquake estimated at magnitude 7.0 damaged about 2,000 buildings and killed about 60 people. It was the largest earthquake ever to hit the eastern United States.

g3_ss.title: South Carolina's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Columbia, Charleston, and the student's town; learn the General Assembly (Senate 46, House 124), the governor, and how judges are chosen; read the state's two mottos.

g3_ss.title: South Carolina's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Catawba, Cherokee, and Cusabo; try a Catawba-style coil pot from clay; learn about the Catawba Indian Nation today.

g3_ss.title: South Carolina Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Timeline cards for Robert Smalls, Morris Brown, and Sergeant William Jasper, plus the Penn School students; students write how each showed courage.

g45_ss.title: South Carolina's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Cofitachequi, Catawba pottery and farming, Cherokee Lower Towns and Keowee, the Cusabo coast, and the Yamasee War.

g45_ss.title: Colony of Rice and Slavery
g45_ss.plan: San Miguel de Gualdape, Charles Town in 1670, the trade in enslaved Native people, the Black majority by 1720, rice and indigo, Gullah culture, and the Revolution at Sullivan's Island.

g45_ss.title: South Carolina 1788–1877
g45_ss.plan: Ratification as the 8th state, Denmark Vesey, the Treaty of Nation Ford, secession and Fort Sumter, Port Royal and Mitchelville, Robert Smalls, the 1868 constitution, and the end of Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: Hurricane Coast
g3_sci.plan: How hurricanes form, the stories of Hugo and Florence, and a family safety kit.

g3_sci.title: Marsh and Island Life
g3_sci.plan: Salt marshes, estuaries, and barrier islands; what lives where fresh and salt water meet.

g3_sci.title: From Mountains to Sea
g3_sci.plan: Build a cross-section model from the Blue Ridge to the Sea Islands, marking the Fall Line and Sandhills.

g45_sci.title: The 1886 Charleston Earthquake
g45_sci.plan: What causes earthquakes, how scientists estimate magnitude, and why the eastern U.S. can still have big quakes.

g45_sci.title: Water Power at the Fall Line
g45_sci.plan: Why rivers drop at the Fall Line, how falling water powered mills, and a simple waterwheel experiment.

g45_sci.title: Rice, Tides, and Knowledge
g45_sci.plan: How West African rice farmers used tides to flood fields, the science of tidal irrigation, and whose knowledge built the Lowcountry.
